study and experience. This chapter covers those conditions, starting with night. About half of Alabama's fatal crashes happen during darkness, even though traffic is light then. In this lesson you will learn how far your headlights reach, why you must never overdrive them, when the law requires you to dim, when headlights are required at all, and the habits that help you see and be seen after dark. Keep a speed at which you can stop within the distance your lights show ahead. Under normal conditions, high beams usually light the road about three hundred fifty feet ahead. So at night, your stopping distance has to fit inside that lighted area. If you are going so fast that you cannot stop within three hundred fifty feet, you will reach a hazard before you can react to it. Keep your lights working and your lenses clean, and keep all glass clean, free of defects and clear of frost and steam. Never drive faster than you can stop within your lights.","fact_ids":["sec11-F03","sec11-F04","sec11-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Dimming and headlight hours","fact_ids":["sec11-F05","sec11-F06","sec11-F08","sec11-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Dim within five hundred and two hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec11-F05","sec11-F06","sec11-F08","sec11-F09"]},{"text":"Headlights from sunset to sunrise.","fact_ids":["sec11-F05","sec11-F06","sec11-F08","sec11-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"The law requires dimming your headlights within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle and within two hundred feet of a vehicle you are following. If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on after you dim, keep yours dimmed anyway, since blinding that driver only endangers you. State law requires headlights, not just parking lights, starting a half-hour after sunset and lasting until a half-hour before sunrise, and also whenever you cannot see clearly for at least five hundred feet. When unsure whether lights are needed, turn them on low beam.","fact_ids":["sec11-F05","sec11-F06","sec11-F08","sec11-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Night habits","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Watch for walkers, bikes, animals.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-F11"]},{"text":"Keep your eyes moving.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"It is hard to see at night, so watch closely for signs, pedestrians, bicycles, slow vehicles and animals, and study maps ahead of time. A companion can act as a second pair of eyes for signs and hazards. Eye fatigue is common in night driving, and moving your eyes from near to far and side to side helps ease it. These habits keep you alert and help you spot hazards sooner. At night, every extra second of warning matters, because your headlights only show a limited distance ahead. Never drive faster than you can stop within your lights. About half of fatal crashes happen in darkness.","fact_ids":["sec11-F10","sec11-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two distances, two rules","fact_ids":["sec11-R01","sec11-F05","sec11-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Dim at five hundred and two hundred.","fact_ids":["sec11-R01","sec11-F05","sec11-F08"]},{"text":"Lights on below five hundred of view.","fact_ids":["sec11-R01","sec11-F05","sec11-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Two different five-hundred-foot rules appear in this lesson. You must dim within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle and within two hundred feet behind a vehicle you are following. Separately, headlights are required whenever you cannot see clearly for five hundred feet ahead. So dim within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and within two hundred feet behind a car, while headlights are required whenever you cannot see five hundred feet ahead. Keep the dimming distances and the visibility distance in their own boxes.","fact_ids":["sec11-R01","sec11-F05","sec11-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check high beam reach","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F03","sec11-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"How far do high beams reach?","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F03","sec11-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: how far ahead do high beams usually light the road under normal conditions? Decide on your answer first. The answer is about three hundred fifty feet. That is why you must never overdrive your headlights: keep a speed at which you can stop within the distance your lights show. If you would need more than about three hundred fifty feet to stop, you are going too fast for the light you have. And remember to dim within five hundred feet of oncoming vehicles and two hundred feet behind others. Never drive faster than you can stop within your lights.","fact_ids":["sec11-F04","sec11-F03","sec11-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Night driving recap","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-F04","sec11-F05","sec11-F06","sec11-F07","sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-F10","sec11-F11","sec11-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop within your lights.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-F04","sec11-F05","sec11-F06","sec11-F07","sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-F10","sec11-F11","sec11-R01"]},{"text":"Dim on time; lights on at dusk.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-F04","sec11-F05","sec11-F06","sec11-F07","sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-F10","sec11-F11","sec11-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, safe driving in changing conditions must be learned, and about half of Alabama's fatal crashes happen in darkness. Never overdrive your headlights; high beams usually reach about three hundred fifty feet. Dim within five hundred feet of oncoming vehicles and two hundred feet behind others, and keep yours dimmed even if others do not. Headlights are required from a half-hour after sunset to a half-hour before sunrise and whenever you cannot see five hundred feet. When unsure, use low beams, keep glass and lenses clean, watch for hazards, and keep your eyes moving.","fact_ids":["sec11-F01","sec11-F02","sec11-F03","sec11-F04","sec11-F05","sec11-F06","sec11-F07","sec11-F08","sec11-F09","sec11-F10","sec11-F11","sec11-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec11-u02","module_id":"sec11-m02","objective_ids":["sec11-u02"],"title":{"text":"Glare, breakdowns, night speed","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F13","sec11-F14"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Glare can blind you for a moment, and night breakdowns put you at risk beside fast traffic.","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F14"]},{"text":"Speed is more dangerous at night because you see less of the road.","fact_ids":["sec11-F16"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Sam's car breaks down on a dark highway.","fact_ids":["sec11-F14"]},"reasoning":{"text":"The manual says to pull well off the road, turn on four-way flashers, raise the hood, and stay with the car if you can.","fact_ids":["sec11-F14"]},"result":{"text":"Sam pulls well off, turns on the flashers, raises the hood and waits with the car.","fact_ids":["sec11-F14","sec11-F15"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking you may drive faster than the limit at night on a road you know well.","fact_ids":["sec11-F16"]},"correction":{"text":"Speed is more dangerous at night because your headlight range does not give enough stopping distance, so obey limits even on familiar roads.","fact_ids":["sec11-F16","sec11-F03"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Eyes right for glare, flashers for breakdowns.","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F14"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You must walk for help after a night breakdown. Where do you walk?","fact_ids":["sec11-F15"]},"answer":{"text":"On the left edge facing traffic, carrying a light.","fact_ids":["sec11-F15"]},"rationale":{"text":"Walking on the left edge facing traffic with a light lets drivers see you and you see them.","fact_ids":["sec11-F15"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Glare and night trouble","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F14","sec11-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Handling glare.","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F14","sec11-F16"]},{"text":"Breakdowns and speed at night.","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F14","sec11-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Glare from other vehicles' lights can seriously impair your vision at night, sometimes to the point of temporary blindness. In this lesson you will learn how to reduce glare from oncoming headlights and from lights behind you, what to do if your car breaks down after dark, how to walk safely if you must leave the car, where to place flares or reflectors, and why speed is more dangerous at night. Night emergencies are worse than daytime ones, because there is less traffic to help, fewer choices and more danger. Night emergencies are worse than daytime ones.","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F14","sec11-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Reducing glare","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Oncoming: look to the right edge.","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F13"]},{"text":"Behind: use the day-night mirror.","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"To cut glare from oncoming lights, look away toward the right edge of the pavement and its white line, so the bright lights are out of the center of your vision. For glare from behind, use a day-night mirror or adjust the mirror to block most of the light. Both methods let you keep driving safely without staring into bright light. Never respond to glare by switching on your own high beams, because blinding the other driver only increases the danger for everyone on the road, including you. Night emergencies are worse than daytime ones. Obey limits even on roads you know.","fact_ids":["sec11-F12","sec11-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Night breakdowns","fact_ids":["sec11-F14","sec11-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pull off; flashers; raise the hood.","fact_ids":["sec11-F14","sec11-F15"]},{"text":"Walk facing traffic; place flares.","fact_ids":["sec11-F14","sec11-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"In a night breakdown, pull well off the road, turn on four-way flashers, raise the hood, and stay with the car if you can. If you must walk, carry a light and walk on the left edge facing traffic. If you have flares or reflectors, place them one hundred to five hundred feet behind the car on the right edge of the highway to warn other traffic. These steps make your car easy to see and keep you out of the path of traffic. Staying with the car is usually safest until help comes. Night emergencies are worse than daytime ones. Obey limits even on roads you know.","fact_ids":["sec11-F14","sec11-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Familiar roads at night","fact_ids":["sec11-F16","sec11-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Obey limits even on known roads.","fact_ids":["sec11-F16","sec11-F03"]},{"text":"Headlights limit stopping distance.","fact_ids":["sec11-F16","sec11-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Drivers who know a road well often think they can safely go faster at night. The manual says speed is more dangerous at night, because at high speed your headlight range does not give enough stopping distance. So obey the posted limits even on roads you know. Familiarity does not let you see farther. A deer, a crash scene or a damaged bridge can appear at the edge of your headlights, and at high speed you will not have room to stop. Night calls for staying within the limit and within your lights. Night emergencies are worse than daytime ones.","fact_ids":["sec11-F16","sec11-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u02-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check walking for help","fact_ids":["sec11-F15","sec11-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"Walking after a breakdown?","fact_ids":["sec11-F15","sec11-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you must walk for help after a night breakdown. Where do you walk? Decide on your answer first. The answer is on the left edge of the road or shoulder, facing traffic, carrying a light. Facing traffic lets you see oncoming vehicles and lets drivers see you. Before you go, remember the other steps: pull well off the road, turn on the four-way flashers and raise the hood, and if you have flares or reflectors, place them one hundred to five hundred feet behind the car on the right edge. Speed is more dangerous at night, so obey limits even on roads you know. driving.","fact_ids":["sec11-F17","sec11-F18","sec11-F24"]}],"narration":{"text":"Winter adds darkness, fog, rain, snow, sleet and ice, and in most cases bad weather alone cannot be blamed for crashes; the driver's response matters more. This lesson covers how to prepare the car before driving, how to find out how slippery the road is, what snow treads and chains can and cannot do, Alabama's law linking wipers and headlights, how far it takes to stop on snow or ice, and how to start and brake smoothly on slippery surfaces. Gentle, early actions are the theme of the whole lesson. Gentle actions keep the tires gripping. Leave far more room on snow or ice.","fact_ids":["sec11-F17","sec11-F18","sec11-F24"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Before you drive","fact_ids":["sec11-F18","sec11-F19","sec11-F20"]},"lines":[{"text":"Warm up while clearing snow and ice.","fact_ids":["sec11-F18","sec11-F19","sec11-F20"]},{"text":"Anti-freeze in the washer fluid.","fact_ids":["sec11-F18","sec11-F19","sec11-F20"]}],"narration":{"text":"Warm the engine while clearing snow and ice from the car and windows, and keep washer fluid mixed with anti-freeze. In extreme cold, avoid using washers at high speed, since the fluid can freeze on the glass and block your view. Once you are moving, test your brakes gently at low speed to learn how slippery the road is, then set your speed to match. These steps let you see clearly and tell you how much grip you really have before you reach higher speeds or busier traffic. Gentle actions keep the tires gripping. Leave far more room on snow or ice.","fact_ids":["sec11-F18","sec11-F19","sec11-F20"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Treads, chains and lights","fact_ids":["sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Treads help in snow, not on ice.","fact_ids":["sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F23"]},{"text":"Wipers on, headlights on.","fact_ids":["sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"Snow treads on the drive wheels improve traction in snow, but you still drive below normal speed and leave more stopping room. Snow treads do not grip ice; for severe ice, hard-packed snow or very deep snow, reinforced tire chains are best. Alabama law requires headlights whenever wipers are running for rain, sleet or snow, but intermittent wiper use does not require them. So equipment helps, but it does not replace slower speeds, and turning on the wipers for falling precipitation means turning on the headlights too. Gentle actions keep the tires gripping.","fact_ids":["sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Starting and stopping","fact_ids":["sec11-F24","sec11-F25","sec11-F26"]},"lines":[{"text":"Three to twelve times the stop.","fact_ids":["sec11-F24","sec11-F25","sec11-F26"]},{"text":"Gentle starts; pump for sudden stops.","fact_ids":["sec11-F24","sec11-F25","sec11-F26"]}],"narration":{"text":"On snow or ice a car needs three to twelve times the stopping distance it needs on dry pavement, so keep well back. To start on snow or ice, keep engine speed very low; with a clutch release it slowly or use second or high gear, and with an automatic accelerate gently. On packed snow or ice brake gently, and for a sudden stop pump the brakes, easing off whenever the wheels lock or start to slip, without pushing in the clutch. Smooth inputs keep the tires gripping instead of spinning or sliding. Gentle actions keep the tires gripping. Leave far more room on snow or ice.","fact_ids":["sec11-F24","sec11-F25","sec11-F26"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Treads are not magic","fact_ids":["sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F24"]},"lines":[{"text":"Snow treads: still slow down.","fact_ids":["sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F24"]},{"text":"On ice, chains are best.","fact_ids":["sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F24"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Drivers with snow treads sometimes feel invincible. Snow treads improve traction in snow, but you still drive below normal speed and leave more stopping room, and they do not grip ice. For severe ice, hard-packed snow or very deep snow, reinforced tire chains are best. And even then, stopping on snow or ice can take three to twelve times the distance it takes on dry pavement. So good equipment is a help, not a reason to keep your normal speed or following distance in winter conditions. Gentle actions keep the tires gripping.","fact_ids":["sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F24"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the wiper law","fact_ids":["sec11-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Wipers and headlights?","fact_ids":["sec11-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: when do Alabama headlights become required because of your wipers? Decide on your answer first. The answer is whenever the wipers are running for rain, sleet or snow. Intermittent use of the wipers does not require headlights. This rule is separate from the darkness rule, which requires headlights from a half-hour after sunset to a half-hour before sunrise. So on a gray, rainy afternoon with the wipers running, your headlights must be on even though it is daytime. Gentle actions keep the tires gripping. Leave far more room on snow or ice.","fact_ids":["sec11-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec11-u03-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Winter recap","fact_ids":["sec11-F17","sec11-F18","sec11-F19","sec11-F20","sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F23","sec11-F24","sec11-F25","sec11-F26"]},"lines":[{"text":"Prepare, test, go gently.","fact_ids":["sec11-F17","sec11-F18","sec11-F19","sec11-F20","sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F23","sec11-F24","sec11-F25","sec11-F26"]},{"text":"Three to twelve times to stop.","fact_ids":["sec11-F17","sec11-F18","sec11-F19","sec11-F20","sec11-F21","sec11-F22","sec11-F23","sec11-F24","sec11-F25","sec11-F26"]}],"narration":{"text":"To sum up, winter adds hazards, but bad weather alone usually is not to blame for crashes. Warm up while clearing snow and ice, use anti-freeze washer fluid, and avoid washers at high speed in extreme cold. Test the brakes gently at low speed.
